While deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in various image understanding tasks, adapting them for detecting urban anomalies remains an underutilized area. This is largely caused by two significant difficulties: first, obtaining adequate training data is hard because anomaly instances are rare by nature, and second, developing a detection model effectively without extensive manual labeling of specific anomaly types is extremely laborious. Addressing these obstacles, we introduce a novel Deep Metric Learning framework designed for anomaly detection in cities that requires no prior knowledge about particular anomalies. By leveraging a small set of "shutter images"—representations of normal city operations—as the baseline, our model self-adapts to identify any irregularities regardless of pre-defined categories. Specifically, we employ an encoder-deeper architecture where the encoder extracts features from standard images, utilizes metric learning to map anomalies into high-dimensional feature space, and applies a rejection strategy to flag outliers. Extensive experiments conducted on two public datasets, along with ablation and comparative studies, confirm that our approach attains competitive benchmark scores.

While theoretical models typically model these processes as ascribing an apparatus an identical property to the measured system, practical implementations inevitably produce measurement errors, a discrepancy that accelerates through non-commutative feedback loops. Consequently, a critical theoretical challenge arises: determining under what conditions an arbitrary joint system-apparatus measurement outcome can be interpreted as a valid physical quantity within the quantum system itself. Addressing this requires extending beyond standard quantum measurement frameworks, as feedback enables measurements in arbitrary bases, in continuous variables, and even probes states lacking natural pointer observables. we introduce a principled framework for optimizing Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) with certifiable robustness guarantees. Utilizing constraint relaxation techniques for non-convex optimization, we adapted the conventional cross-entropy loss to ensure posterior robustness against worst-case $\epsilon$-ball perturbations. This discrepancy stems in part from standard training approaches, which often fail to consider how individual weights, inputs, and activations specifically behave under the non-linear constraints of quantization. excitonic insulator, characterized by bound electron-hole pairs, holds significant importance in condensed matter physics. We contend that the conventional criterion for describing this transition relies on approximations that obscure the precise boundary between the paired states and charged carriers involved. In this study, we analyze the critical condition based on physical principles and derive a novel formula. This approach involves comparing the chemical potential to the bound energy of the pairs and results in a simpler determination of the transition point. Notably, our method not only simplifies calculations but also clarifies the nature of the electron pair binding in semimetals through its logical theoretical foundation. In this specific context, we have identified that the bound electron pairs reside at zero energy relative to the chemical potential when the semimetal transitions to an insulator state. Based on our derived formal criteria for this transition, we applied it to certain semimetal materials within the doped graphene system and identified Aharonov-Ohm rings as suitable candidates. In these structures, we demonstrated how to experimentally verify the critical condition by examining the $0/T_B$ ratio (where $T_B$ is the binding temperature and $T_B/T_F$ is the binding temperature relative to the Fermi temperature). This experimental validation supports the accuracy and utility of our proposed method.

To tackle the initial challenge, the study introduces two novel attack methodologies. The initial approach, an active search technique, uniquely integrates multiple instances of detection models to enhance search efficacy and avoid getting trapped in local optima; furthermore, artificial boundary constraints are imposed on the search area to increase the likelihood of successfully detecting objects. Experimental results confirm that this method achieves superior accuracy across various existing benchmarks. The second proposed method is an unsupervised generation technique capable of creating high-quality adversarial perturbations with significantly higher computational efficiency compared to the first approach. Additionally, this method can synthesize threats targeting specific, customized datasets that do not overlap with the training data used to build the neural network. Capabilities of this generation process are validated across diverse benchmarking scenarios to demonstrate effectiveness. The second part of the research focuses on defensive solutions; the authors propose a novel architecture that is more robust against adversarial perturbations by incorporating multiple detection models to aggregate their outputs in a weighted manner. This "ensemble-based" framework demonstrates enhanced robustness through empirical evaluation. The study concludes by presenting comprehensive experimental analyses to substantiate these findings and validate the proposed approaches.

visual quality and rendering performance of line segments in 3D systems. While traditional anti-aliasing strategies rely on computing how line segments intersect individual screen pixels and using weight values to adjust color based on this overlap, a significant challenge arises when handling very fine line segments. When such thin lines occupy fewer than three pixels on a standard display, color calculation becomes a problem, often leading to either performance bottlenecks due to excessive screenwriter calls or visible banding artifacts. To resolve this, we present an approach designed for real-time application that avoids determining exact overlaps between segments and pixels altogether. Instead, we distribute the segment's color across all pixels that the segment passes through within specific sub-regions, ensuring that the cumulative weight across any window summing to total one is maintained. By integrating this method into a hardware-friendly Hessian filter bank constructed from discrete wavelet transforms (DWT), we eliminate the need to calculate overlap values directly. Instead, we determine the final pixel color through weighted accumulation within localized windows. This strategy ensures that computational complexity grows linearly with model complexity and maintains high processing efficiency by fully exploiting data locality and minimizing memory access latency.
